title: Picture graphs: count, don't just look
hook: Young children compare picture graphs by which row looks longest. That only works if every picture is the same size and every row starts from the same line.
coreIdeaMd:
A picture graph shows **one picture for each item** (one-to-one).

- Every picture should be the **same size**, lined up from the **same starting line**.
- Then the longest row really is the biggest group.
- If the pictures are different sizes, children need to **count**, not judge by length.

Start with real objects (children standing in lines for their favourite fruit), then pictures, then simple graphs.
workedExampleMd:
**Favourite pets in a class of 19.**

| Pet | Count |
|---|---|
| Dog | 8 |
| Cat | 6 |
| Fish | 5 |

1. Make a picture graph with one same-sized picture per child, rows starting from one line.
2. The dog row is longest, and the count agrees: 8 is the most.
3. Ask: "How many more chose dog than fish?" Children can match the rows picture by picture to see 3 more.

checkItems.stemMd: In a picture graph, the row for cats looks longer than the row for dogs, but the cat pictures are drawn bigger. How should you decide which pet was more popular?
options: Count the pictures in each row
Choose the row with bigger pictures
checkItems.answer: Count the pictures in each row
checkItems.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Each picture stands for one choice, so counting tells you which has more.
checkItems.feedbackIncorrect: When pictures are different sizes, the row length can trick you. Count the pictures: each one is one choice.

wrongAnswers.feedback: Length only works when every picture is the same size. Here the cat pictures are bigger, so count the pictures in each row instead.

tryTomorrow: Make a quick class picture graph with sticky notes of the same size, then make one with mixed sizes. Ask: "Which graph is fair? Why?"
reflectPrompt: How do your students currently show you how they compared two groups?
